fable-5.1.text:
I think what I valued most, looking back, was how much it emphasized fundamentals over anything trendy. When I was there, machine learning wasn't the hot thing it is now. Most of what we did was algorithms, theory of computation, operating systems, compilers, that kind of core material. At the time I probably didn't appreciate it fully, but it gave me a way of thinking about problems that has stayed with me, whether I'm working on reinforcement learning or on language models.

The other thing was the peer group. The curriculum itself was rigorous, but honestly a lot of the learning happened outside the classroom, with classmates who were just incredibly sharp and curious. You'd be working on an assignment at two in the morning and arguing about the right way to approach it, and that kind of pressure and collaboration pushes you more than any single course does.

And there was enough flexibility in the later years to explore. I remember taking a few courses that touched on AI and natural language, which was a fairly niche interest then, and that's really what nudged me toward research and eventually grad school. So I'd say it was the combination of a strong theoretical foundation, a great set of people, and just enough room to find what you actually cared about.

r001.rationale: The response credits IIT Madras’s coverage of algorithms, theory of computation, operating systems, compilers, and other core material with giving him a strong, broadly applicable foundation for later work in reinforcement learning and language models.

opus-5.5.text:
I think what I valued most was how strong the fundamentals were. The curriculum was very rigorous on the core: algorithms, data structures, discrete math, theory of computation, operating systems, compilers. At the time some of it felt quite theoretical, and you wondered when you'd use it. But looking back, that foundation is what lets you pick up new areas quickly. When I moved into machine learning and NLP, so much came down to thinking clearly about algorithms and complexity, and being comfortable with the math. That came from those years.

The other thing was the peer group. You're surrounded by really sharp, motivated people, and a lot of the learning happens outside the classroom: late-night discussions, working through problem sets together, programming contests, side projects. That culture pushes you to hold yourself to a high bar.

And toward the later years I got some exposure to research through projects with faculty. That's where I first got a taste of open-ended problems where there isn't a known answer at the back of the book. That shift from solving well-defined problems to asking your own questions was a big part of why I went on to do a PhD. So it was the mix of a really solid technical core and the chance to start exploring research that I'd say I appreciated most.

r001.rationale: The response describes a rigorous curriculum spanning algorithms, data structures, discrete math, theory, operating systems, and compilers, and explicitly says this foundation enabled learning new areas such as machine learning and NLP.

fable-5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, looking back, what I really valued about IIT Madras was how strongly it emphasized fundamentals. The curriculum wasn't chasing whatever was trendy at the time — it was grounded in the core of computer science: algorithms, theory of computation, operating systems, computer architecture. You really built things up from first principles, and there was a lot of mathematical rigor baked into everything. At the time, honestly, some of it felt abstract — you'd wonder why you were proving properties of automata when you wanted to build software. But that foundation turned out to be incredibly durable. Technologies come and go, especially in a field like machine learning where the landscape shifts every couple of years, but the ability to think rigorously about a problem, to reason about complexity and abstraction — that never goes out of date.

The other thing I'd point to is the peer group. You're surrounded by people who are genuinely curious and very driven, and a lot of the learning happened outside the classroom — late-night discussions, working on projects together, pushing each other. That environment teaches you how to learn on your own, which is arguably the most important skill, because so much of what I've done since — NLP, deep learning — wasn't really part of the curriculum back then. The curriculum gave me the tools to pick those things up myself.

r001.rationale: The response credits IIT Madras's curriculum with emphasizing computer-science fundamentals across algorithms, theory of computation, operating systems, and computer architecture, describing it as a durable foundation.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, the thing I appreciate most in hindsight is how unfashionable it was. This was the mid-2000s, and there was no machine learning course to speak of — maybe one elective that was mostly classical AI, search, logic, that sort of thing. What we got instead was a very heavy dose of fundamentals: algorithms, theory of computation, compilers, operating systems, computer architecture. And not in a survey way — you actually built a compiler, you actually wrote a small OS kernel in the lab courses. There was this assumption baked into the curriculum that you should be able to go down to the metal if you had to.

At the time I remember feeling a bit impatient about it. Why am I doing register allocation when there's all this interesting stuff happening on the web? But that foundation turned out to be the most durable thing I took away. The specific frameworks I learned in grad school are all dead now. The ability to look at a system and reason about what it's actually doing computationally — that hasn't depreciated at all. A lot of what we do in large-scale training is, frankly, systems work wearing a machine learning hat.

The other part, which isn't really curriculum, is the people. You're surrounded by a few hundred students who are all intensely curious and somewhat competitive, and you learn an enormous amount just from the hostel conversations. That ambient pressure to understand things properly, rather than just well enough to pass — I don't think I've found a substitute for it since.

r001.rationale: The response credits IIT Madras’s curriculum with a durable foundation and lists broad coverage across algorithms, theory, compilers, operating systems, and computer architecture.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think what I valued most was how strong the fundamentals were. We had a lot of core coursework: data structures, algorithms, theory of computation, operating systems, architecture. You couldn't skip any of it. At the time some of it felt like a grind, but it gave me a mental toolkit that I still use. When I'm debugging a training pipeline, or thinking about why a method does or doesn't scale, I'm often falling back on intuitions from those basic courses.

The other thing was the peer group. Everyone around you was incredibly driven and smart, and much of the learning happened outside class, in late-night discussions, working through problem sets together, and building projects just because someone thought it would be fun. That culture of pushing each other made a big difference.

The curriculum also didn't tie you to any particular technology. It was less "learn this framework" and more "learn how to think about problems," so when I later moved into machine learning and NLP, which weren't a big part of what I studied, I could pick them up. I think that's the best thing a curriculum can do: teach you how to learn the next thing yourself.

r001.rationale: The response credits IIT Madras’s strong, wide-ranging core coursework—including algorithms, theory, operating systems, and architecture—with giving the speaker a lasting foundational mental toolkit in computer science.

What I really valued was the grounding in fundamentals. You’re learning algorithms, theory, systems—different ways of thinking about computation—and not just how to use a particular programming language or tool. Those foundations stay useful even as the technology changes.

I also appreciated getting exposure to different areas of computer science before having to decide what I wanted to focus on. You start to see the connections between subjects, and that gives you a basis for exploring new problems. For me, that’s an important part of an undergraduate education: learning how to think through something unfamiliar, rather than just learning the things you already know you want to do.
